newsitem.title: USA: South Carolina economy grows at twice national rate.
newsitem.headline: South Carolina economy grows at twice national rate.

text.p: South Carolina's gross state product grew 4.9 percent in the last year, more than twice the national rate of 2.3 percent, First Union economist Mark Vitner said Wednesday.
He spoke at the Local Government Investment and Debt Training Conference sponsored by the state treasurer's office.
Although the state economy is expected to slow in 1997, "We expect South Carolina to outperform the rest of the nation, with about a 4 percent growth rate," Vitner said.

South Carolina would have done even better this year if not for the continuing downsizing at the Savannah River Plant and the layoffs at Charleston Naval Shipyard, he said. The state's private sector grew 6.2 percent for the year.
Vitner said South Carolina's manufacturing sector continued to expand, although its growth rate slowed to about 2.3 percent in the past year because of declines in textiles and apparel.

The state saw strong gains in machinery, transportation equipment and chemicals, partly because of export growth. Exports in manufactured goods rose 8.2 percent during the year. Tourism grew by 6.9 percent over last year.

Regionally, Vitner said the Upstate, while bedeviled by 10 percent employment cuts in textiles and apparel, is expected to post 2.2 percent job growth this year. Columbia will come close, with growth of about 2 percent.
Charleston will post growth of about 1 percent this year, as strong private sector growth has more than offset the shutdown of the Charleston Naval Base.
Vitner said the strongest gains were in Hilton Head and Myrtle Beach, where job gains topped 5.2 percent due to tourism and migration from other states.
Corporate relocations to South Carolina have also boosted the state economy, especially in Rock Hill, York County, Greenwood and Florence, he said.

He predicted statewide holiday spending would rise by 8 percent over last year, with clothing accounting for a large part of purchases. He said computers and home electronics will do well, but their gains will trail prior years.
